options.D: Store all household cleaning supplies inside the bedroom wardrobe.

explanation: Falls are a huge risk for patients with low vision. Clearing out tripping hazards like loose rugs and keeping hallways bright makes their home environment much safer!

question: Which of these is NOT a safe way for a visually impaired patient to tell different medicine bottles apart?

options.A: Using distinct physical shapes or textured bumps on bottle caps
options.B: Asking a trusted family member to organize and label the medications
options.C: Reading the standard small-print label by dim bedside candlelight
options.D: Placing tactile rubber bands around specific prescription containers

explanation: Trying to read tiny print in dim light is a recipe for a medication error if you have low vision! Using touch-based methods like rubber bands or textured caps is much safer.

question: Which healthcare professional specializes in testing hearing and fitting hearing aids?

options.A: Ophthalmologist
options.B: Audiologist
options.C: Dietitian
options.D: Podiatrist

explanation: An audiologist is the expert you call for hearing tests, ear diagnoses, and finding the right hearing devices for patients. Easy to remember!

question: What is the primary role of the nurse when working with a patient who needs multi-specialty sensory care?

options.A: Manufacturing custom hearing aids for patients in the hospital ward
options.B: Acting as a central coordinator to connect the patient with various specialists
options.C: Replacing the need for occupational therapy visits in the home
options.D: Performing complex eye surgeries alongside the primary surgeon

explanation: Nurses act as the glue of the healthcare team! We coordinate care plans, help the patient understand referrals, and make sure everyone is on the same page.

question: What is the primary goal of aseptic technique in nursing practice?

options.A: Eliminating all water in the room
options.B: Speeding up the patient discharge process
options.C: Minimizing pathogen contamination
options.D: Reducing the cost of hospital stays

explanation: Aseptic techniques are specifically designed practices that keep patients free from harmful disease-causing microbes during care. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h1)

question: How does aseptic technique differ from everyday household cleaning?

options.A: Aseptic technique is only performed by medical doctors
options.B: Aseptic technique aims for the complete absence of disease-producing microbes
options.C: Household cleaning uses stronger bleach solutions than hospitals
options.D: Household cleaning is regulated by strict international health laws

explanation: While cleaning removes visible dirt, aseptic technique specifically targets invisible pathogens to protect patients during vulnerable procedures. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h1)

question: Medical asepsis is also commonly referred to by which term?

options.A: Sterile technique
options.B: Clean technique
options.C: Barrier protection
options.D: Surgical isolation

explanation: Medical asepsis focuses on reducing the number of microbes and is widely known as clean technique in daily nursing tasks. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h2)

question: A nurse is preparing to insert an indwelling urinary catheter. Which type of technique must be used?

options.A: Surgical asepsis
options.B: Universal decontamination
options.C: Standard sanitation
options.D: Medical asepsis

explanation: Catheterization enters the sterile urinary tract, requiring surgical asepsis to prevent introducing bacteria into the bladder. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h2)

question: What happens when a sterile item touches a non-sterile surface?

options.A: It is instantly contaminated
options.B: It is safe to use if dry
options.C: It can be wiped with alcohol to fix it
options.D: It remains sterile for one hour

explanation: The moment a sterile object touches anything not sterile, its sterile state is broken and it cannot be used. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h3)

question: Why must sterile fields and items always be kept above waist level?

options.A: Hospital policies dictate that lower shelves are for waste
options.B: Gravity pulls heavier dust particles upward toward the chest
options.C: It prevents back strain during prolonged surgical procedures
options.D: Items below the waist are out of the nurse's direct line of sight

explanation: Anything below the waist or out of vision cannot be reliably monitored for contamination, so it is treated as unsterile. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is considered the single most effective way to stop the spread of infection?

options.A: Wearing sterile gowns
options.B: Hand hygiene
options.C: Routine room painting
options.D: Using plastic aprons

explanation: Proper handwashing or alcohol rub use removes transient microbes from hands, preventing cross-contamination between patients. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h4)

question: Standard precautions must be applied to which group of patients?

options.A: Only patients with confirmed blood-borne viruses
options.B: Patients admitted to the surgical ward only
options.C: All patients regardless of their diagnosis
options.D: Individuals showing visible signs of a fever

explanation: Standard precautions assume any patient fluid could carry pathogens, protecting nurses and patients alike during every encounter. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which piece of personal protective equipment is put on last when preparing for a sterile procedure?

options.A: Cap
options.B: Gloves
options.C: Gown
options.D: Mask

explanation: Gloves are always donned last so they remain clean and do not touch other equipment during the gowning and masking process. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of wearing a face mask and protective eyewear during certain procedures?

options.A: Keeping the nurse's face warm in cold operating rooms
options.B: Preventing the patient from seeing the nurse's facial expressions
options.C: Protecting mucous membranes from splashes of body fluids
options.D: Filtering out all oxygen molecules in the room

explanation: Masks and goggles create a barrier against blood or fluid splashes that could enter through the eyes, nose, or mouth. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h5)

question: Which part of an opened sterile wrapper is considered non-sterile?

options.A: The outer one-inch border
options.B: The inner contents of the tray
options.C: The top layer of the packaging
options.D: The exact center of the drape

explanation: The outer inch touches unsterile surfaces or hands when opening, making it unsafe to consider sterile. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why must a prepared sterile field never be left unattended by the nurse?

options.A: Sterile drapes have a tendency to blow away in room drafts
options.B: Contamination can occur unnoticed if no one is watching the field
options.C: Hospital security regulations forbid empty treatment rooms
options.D: Patients might try to steal the surgical instruments

explanation: Leaving a field unsupervised risks unseen breaches in sterility, which compromises patient safety if used. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h6)

question: A nurse is changing a dressing on a large surgical abdominal wound. What is the primary reason for using sterile instruments and supplies?

options.A: To make the dressing change process faster and easier
options.B: To prevent bacteria from entering the open surgical wound
options.C: To stop the patient from feeling pain during the procedure
options.D: To remove old scar tissue from previous operations

explanation: Open wounds are direct pathways for bacteria to cause local infection or systemic sepsis, making sterile tools essential. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h7)

question: What does the abbreviation HAI stand for in nursing practice?

options.A: High acuity illness
options.B: Hygiene assessment indicator
options.C: Healthcare-associated infection
options.D: Hospital antiseptic index

explanation: HAIs are infections patients acquire while receiving medical treatment in a hospital or clinic facility. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h8)

question: Which observation is an early sign of a localized wound infection that a nurse should report?

options.A: Normal pale pink skin around sutures
options.B: Lowered blood pressure readings
options.C: Increased appetite and weight gain
options.D: Purulent drainage and local warmth

explanation: Pus and warmth around a wound site indicate active inflammation and bacterial infection requiring prompt intervention. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h8)

question: What is the main reason we use stitches to close a simple skin cut?

options.A: To reduce healing time and minimize scarring
options.B: To stop deep muscle spasms near the injury site
options.C: To permanently eliminate all risk of bacterial infection
options.D: To replace the need for a tetanus toxoid booster

explanation: You've got this! Bringing the skin edges neatly together helps the cut heal much faster and keeps the scar as small as possible. Great job!

question: Why must you check when a patient had their last tetanus shot before stitching up a wound?

options.A: To determine if the patient needs protection against tetanus spores in dirty wounds
options.B: To check how fast the patient's blood will normally clot
options.C: To decide what type of local anesthetic to inject
options.D: To calculate the exact day the sutures should be removed

explanation: Cuts can easily trap dirt and tetanus bacteria. Checking their history helps us know if they need a booster shot to stay safe. Simple and lifesaving!

question: Which tool do nurses use to hold and guide a suture needle securely through the skin?

options.A: Suture scissors
options.B: Needle holder
options.C: Tissue forceps
options.D: Scalpel handle

explanation: Spot on! A needle holder has special grip jaws built to hold a curved needle firmly so it doesn't slip or bend while you work.

question: Where should you NEVER inject a local painkiller (anesthetic) that contains adrenaline?

options.A: On the tip of the nose or fingers
options.B: Across the front of the thigh
options.C: On the fleshy part of the upper back
options.D: Along a straight scalp laceration

explanation: Adrenaline makes blood vessels squeeze shut. In delicate areas like fingers and noses, this can completely cut off blood supply and damage the tissue. Good to know for clinical practice!

question: What is the best way to wash loose dirt and germs out of a fresh cut?

options.A: Soaking the entire wound in a tub of tap water
options.B: Scrubbing the inside of the cut with dry gauze
options.C: High-pressure irrigation using normal saline
options.D: Applying strong antiseptic solution directly into the tissue

explanation: Using a syringe with sterile saline creates just enough gentle pressure to wash away debris without harming the healing flesh. You're building great clinical skills!

question: Why should you avoid pouring harsh surgical scrubs directly inside an open wound?

options.A: It can damage exposed tissue cells and delay proper wound healing
options.B: It instantly inactivates any local anesthetic you inject later
options.C: It permanently stains the surrounding skin a bright yellow color
options.D: It causes the skin edges to swell up and prevent knot tying

explanation: Harsh chemicals are too strong for delicate exposed cells inside a wound. Stick to normal saline for cleaning—your patients will heal much better!

question: Which type of thread is used for outer skin stitches and needs to be taken out after a few days?

options.A: Absorbable suture
options.B: Non-absorbable suture
options.C: Catgut suture
options.D: Biodegradable thread

explanation: Non-absorbable materials like nylon give strong outer support while the skin heals, and we remove them during a follow-up visit. Easypz!

question: What is the big advantage of using a cutting needle when stitching tough skin?

options.A: Its sharp edge easily pierces through tough dermal layers
options.B: It stops the wound from bleeding during the procedure
options.C: It prevents the patient from feeling any sharp pain
options.D: It dissolves safely inside the body tissue after a week

explanation: Skin can be surprisingly tough! Cutting needles have a sharp edge designed to glide smoothly through without bending. You're mastering instrument basics.

question: At what angle should your needle enter the skin to create a smooth, curved stitch?

options.A: A downward 45-degree angle
options.B: A flat 15-degree angle
options.C: A completely parallel angle
options.D: A perpendicular 90-degree angle

explanation: Entering at a 90-degree angle lets the curved needle follow its natural circular shape, making it glide right through the skin smoothly.

question: Where should your finished knot sit after tying a simple interrupted stitch?

options.A: Tucked tightly underneath the tissue forceps
options.B: Off to the side of the incision line
options.C: Buried deep underneath the subcutaneous fat layer
options.D: Directly in the center of the open wound gap

explanation: Always pull your knot off to the side! This keeps it from pressing down directly into the healing cut and causing irritation. Perfect technique!

question: Why do we usually remove facial stitches much sooner than stitches on the leg?

options.A: Facial skin heals slower and requires longer support
options.B: Facial sutures are always made of absorbable material
options.C: The face has a rich blood supply and skin marks easily
options.D: Legs experience much less daily movement than the face

explanation: The face gets loads of blood supply, so it heals super fast. Taking stitches out early also prevents ugly cross-hatch marks on the skin!

question: A patient had a deep cut on their shin stitched 8 days ago and asks to remove the stitches. What do you tell them?

options.A: Yes, because leg wounds heal faster than any other body part
options.B: Yes, all sutures can safely come out after exactly seven days
options.C: No, sutures must stay in place for at least a full month
options.D: No, limb and joint wounds usually need ten to fourteen days of healing support

explanation: Areas over joints or shins move a lot and have less blood flow, so they need 10 to 14 days before taking stitches out. Safety first!

question: Which sign tells you right away that a stitched wound might be getting infected?

options.A: Purulent drainage and spreading warmth
options.B: Firm skin edges held closely together
options.C: Mild itching around the knot after three days
options.D: A slight pink border immediately after suturing

explanation: Pus (purulent drainage) and skin that feels warm to the touch are classic warning signs that bacteria are multiplying in the wound. Great clinical catch!

question: What is the medical term used when a stitched wound unexpectedly pops open?

options.A: Dehiscence
options.B: Cellulitis
options.C: Hematoma
options.D: Necrosis

explanation: When a wound separates or pops open, we call it dehiscence. It usually happens if there's too much tension or movement before the tissue heals. You're learning pro terminology!

question: What is the very first priority when a patient arrives in the emergency department with a severe laceration?

options.A: Checking airway, breathing, and circulation
options.B: Administering local anesthesia
options.C: Choosing the right suture material
options.D: Cleaning the wound with iodine

explanation: General patient stability and life-threatening issues always come before treating localized injuries like skin lacerations. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is it important to test movement and feeling in the fingers or toes below a wound before stitching it?

options.A: To make the skin easier to numb with medication
options.B: To prevent the wound from becoming infected later
options.C: To see if the patient is allergic to local anesthetics
options.D: To check if nerves and blood vessels were damaged by the injury

explanation: Testing distal motor and sensory function helps catch nerve or vessel damage early, before any repair work begins. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which medication is most commonly used as a local anesthetic for closing minor wounds?

options.A: Lignocaine
options.B: Paracetamol
options.C: Morphine
options.D: Diazepam

explanation: Lignocaine numbs the local area quickly and safely when administered correctly before suturing. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h2)

question: Where should a nurse NOT use a local anesthetic mixed with adrenaline?

options.A: On a clean scalp wound
options.B: On a forearm abrasion
options.C: On a large thigh laceration
options.D: On the fingers or toes

explanation: Adrenaline causes blood vessels to constrict tightly, which can cut off blood supply entirely in digits and lead to tissue death. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of irrigating a fresh wound with normal saline?

options.A: To wash away bacteria and loose debris
options.B: To numb the pain temporarily
options.C: To close the skin edges tightly
options.D: To stop bleeding from large arteries

explanation: High-volume fluid irrigation physically flushes out contaminants that could otherwise cause a localized infection. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why do emergency personnel perform debridement on a ragged, torn wound before stitching it?

options.A: It makes the skin numb to the pain of the needle
options.B: Dead tissue delays healing and easily breeds bacteria
options.C: It stops the patient from feeling nervous
options.D: It stretches the skin so fewer stitches are needed

explanation: Removing non-viable tissue leaves only healthy, bleeding tissue that can heal rapidly and resist infection. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which type of needle is best suited for piercing tough, thick outer skin?

options.A: Blunt needle
options.B: Spatula needle
options.C: Tapered needle
options.D: Cutting needle

explanation: Cutting needles have a sharp edge specifically designed to pass through tough dermal layers without bending. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h4)

question: A patient requires skin closure on a forehead laceration that will need stitches removed in five days. Which suture type should the nurse prepare?

options.A: Absorbable gut
options.B: Elastic band material
options.C: Non-absorbable nylon
options.D: Heavy wire suture

explanation: Skin surface closures require non-absorbable materials like nylon so they remain intact until manual removal. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the most common and versatile suturing technique used for simple emergency lacerations?

options.A: Retention bridge stitch
options.B: Simple interrupted suture
options.C: Subcuticular continuous stitch
options.D: Continuous running lock

explanation: Simple interrupted stitches are quick to place and provide reliable closure where each stitch stands alone. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why should a surgical knot be positioned to the side of the wound incision rather than directly over it?

options.A: To make it easier for the patient to pull out later
options.B: To prevent pressure on the wound line that can slow healing
options.C: To ensure the local anesthetic stays active longer
options.D: To save suture material during the procedure

explanation: Placing knots off-center prevents direct pressure and irritation on the healing skin edge underneath. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of normal wound healing that a patient should expect?

options.A: A thin line of pinkness near the cut
options.B: Pus draining from the incision site
options.C: Dry scabbing along the suture line
options.D: Mild tenderness around the edges

explanation: Pus indicates a bacterial infection and is never a normal part of wound healing. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h6)

question: Why do facial stitches need to be removed much sooner than stitches on a knee or back?

options.A: Facial skin is much thicker than skin on the back
options.B: The face heals faster due to a rich blood supply
options.C: Stitches on the face cause less scarring if left longer
options.D: Facial muscles do not move during daily activities

explanation: The abundant blood supply in the head and neck allows rapid healing, requiring early suture removal to prevent track marks. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is a superficial abscess?

options.A: A widespread bacterial infection of the entire muscle layer
options.B: A painless fluid-filled blister caused by a minor burn
options.C: A localized collection of pus in the skin or subcutaneous tissue
options.D: A non-inflammatory hard knot under the skin surface

explanation: An abscess is a walled-off pocket of pus that forms under the skin in response to a localized bacterial invasion. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h1)

question: When assessing a skin boil or abscess, which physical sign tells you it is soft, filled with liquid, and ready for drainage?

options.A: Local pallor
options.B: Cool skin temperature
options.C: Fluctuation
options.D: Complete skin numbness

explanation: Fluctuation is just the clinical term for when the center feels bouncy or squishy under your fingers—that tells you liquid pus has gathered inside and it's ready to be let out!

question: Before you start draining an uncomfortable abscess, what piece of patient history is most crucial to check?

options.A: Blood type classification
options.B: Recent dietary preferences
options.C: Allergies to local anesthetics
options.D: History of childhood asthma

explanation: Always check for anesthetic allergies first! You want to keep your patient comfortable and pain-free without triggering a bad drug reaction.

question: A patient has a painful abscess right over the palm of their wrist, dangerously close to major nerves and blood vessels. What should you do first?

options.A: Apply hot compresses and send the patient home
options.B: Start high-dose oral antibiotics without any drainage
options.C: Immediately perform bedside incision and drainage
options.D: Refer the patient for specialized surgical evaluation

explanation: Hands and faces have delicate nerves and blood vessels. Abscesses in these tricky spots are best left to specialists to avoid accidental permanent injury.

question: During an abscess drainage procedure, what is the main reason the nurse or doctor uses a hemostat?

options.A: Making the initial sharp skin incision
options.B: Blunt dissection to break up pus pockets
options.C: Suturing the wound tightly shut
options.D: Scrubbing the skin free of bacteria

explanation: You gently insert closed hemostats into the cavity and open them up to break through tiny internal walls, making sure all trapped pockets of pus can drain out freely.

question: Why is wearing a face shield so important when you are about to drain an abscess?

options.A: To keep the sterile instrument tray completely dry
options.B: To reduce the patient's anxiety during local numbing
options.C: To prevent accidental splashes of infected pus and blood
options.D: To filter out room dust from entering the open cavity

explanation: Pus inside an abscess is often under pressure. When the incision is made, it can squirt unexpectedly—protecting your eyes and face is a must!

question: Why does injecting local numbing medicine directly into the middle of an inflamed abscess often not work very well?

options.A: The acidic environment of the pus neutralizes the local anesthetic
options.B: The nerve endings in the center are already permanently destroyed
options.C: The pus pressure pushes the medication back out the needle hole
options.D: The thick skin blocks the numbing medicine from spreading

explanation: Infected, pus-filled areas have an acidic chemistry that stops the numbing medicine from doing its job. That is why doctors usually numb the healthy skin around the edges instead!

question: When making the initial cut to drain an abscess, which direction should the surgical blade follow?

options.A: Directly perpendicular to muscle fibers
options.B: In a randomized zigzag pattern
options.C: Along the natural skin tension lines
options.D: In a wide circular shape around the border

explanation: Cutting along the body's natural skin lines (Langer's lines) helps the wound heal better and keeps scarring to a minimum.

question: If an abscess cavity has been packed with gauze, when is the patient usually asked to return for a check-up?

options.A: In one month for suture removal
options.B: Only if severe pain returns
options.C: After exactly two full weeks
options.D: Within 24 to 48 hours

explanation: Patients with packed wounds need a quick follow-up in 1 to 2 days so the healthcare team can check the healing and start removing the packing material.

question: A patient comes back two days after an abscess drainage with a fever and redness that is spreading outward from the wound. What does this mean?

options.A: Worsening infection requiring prompt medical reassessment
options.B: An allergic reaction to the cotton inside the dressing
options.C: Successful eradication of all bacteria from the body
options.D: Normal healing response as the deep tissues close

explanation: Spreading redness and fever are warning signs that the infection is fighting back and traveling further. The patient needs a doctor to take a look right away.

question: Why are antibiotics often NOT needed after successfully draining a simple, small skin abscess?

options.A: The body destroys the remaining bacteria within minutes
options.B: Antibiotics cannot travel through the blood to skin tissues
options.C: Skin bacteria are naturally immune to all oral medications
options.D: Physical removal of the pus cures the localized infection

explanation: Once you drain the trapped pus out of a simple abscess, the body's natural immune system is usually strong enough to take care of the rest all on its own!

question: Which of these is NOT a good reason to prescribe antibiotics along with draining an abscess?

options.A: The presence of severe surrounding skin redness and swelling
options.B: The patient developing a fever and systemic chills
options.C: The patient simply prefers taking pills over wound care
options.D: The patient having a compromised immune system

explanation: Antibiotics are powerful drugs reserved for spreading infections, fevers, or weak immune systems—never just because a patient prefers taking pills over doing proper wound care.

question: What part of the male genitalia is removed during circumcision?

options.A: The urethral meatus
options.B: The foreskin
options.C: The penile shaft skin
options.D: The scrotal sac

explanation: Circumcision specifically involves surgically excising the prepuce, or foreskin, that covers the glans penis. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why do public health organizations strongly support male circumcision in many regions?

options.A: It stops the natural production of testosterone
options.B: It permanently eliminates the need for personal hygiene
options.C: It completely cures all forms of urinary tract infections
options.D: It helps reduce the transmission of HIV and other infections

explanation: Great job! Medical studies show that male circumcision significantly lowers the risk of contracting HIV and certain other sexually transmitted infections, making it a key public health tool.

question: What is the name of the delicate strip of skin on the underside of the penis that connects to the foreskin?

options.A: Corona
options.B: Preputial sac
options.C: Frenulum
options.D: Dorsal vein

explanation: Spot on! The frenulum is that sensitive little band of tissue underneath the penis. Surgeons take great care here because it has a rich blood supply.

question: Why is knowing the location of the dorsal penile nerves important during a circumcision?

options.A: It controls the blood flow to the entire lower abdomen
options.B: It guides where to give a local nerve block for pain relief
options.C: It helps prevent accidental removal of the urethral opening
options.D: It ensures the scrotal skin heals without any scarring

explanation: You've got this! Doctors inject local numbing medication near these dorsal nerves on top of the penis to block pain signals effectively and keep the baby comfortable.

question: What do we call the condition where the foreskin is too tight and cannot be pulled back over the glans?

options.A: Balanitis
options.B: Cryptorchidism
options.C: Phimosis
options.D: Hypospadias

explanation: Phimosis means the foreskin is tight and cannot be easily retracted (pulled back). This is one of the common medical reasons a circumcision might be needed later in life.

question: A newborn is scheduled for circumcision, but you notice the urethral opening is on the underside of the penis. What should you do?

options.A: Report the finding and hold the procedure because the foreskin may be needed for future repair
options.B: Apply an antiseptic ointment and wrap the penis tightly in gauze
options.C: Proceed with the circumcision quickly before the doctor arrives
options.D: Reassure the mother that this is a normal variation

explanation: This condition is called hypospadias. Always hold off on circumcision and report it—surgeons actually need that extra foreskin tissue to reconstruct the urethra later!

question: What is an important nursing check before preparing an infant for a scheduled circumcision?

options.A: Starting an intravenous line in the foot
options.B: Checking when the baby last fed
options.C: Shaving the entire pubic and scrotal hair
options.D: Administering a full dose of oral antibiotics

explanation: Checking the last feeding time helps prevent the baby from vomiting and potentially choking (aspirating) while being handled during the procedure.

question: Why is asking about family bleeding history so important before a circumcision?

options.A: To check if the patient is allergic to local numbing medications
options.B: To determine the correct antibiotic cream to apply after surgery
options.C: To predict how fast the surgical wound will grow new skin cells
options.D: To screen for clotting disorders like hemophilia that could cause excessive bleeding

explanation: Safety first! Screening for bleeding disorders helps catch conditions like hemophilia early, preventing dangerous and uncontrolled bleeding after the cut is made.

question: Which circumcision tool uses a small plastic ring tied over the foreskin that eventually falls off on its own?

options.A: Plastibell
options.B: Gomco clamp
options.C: Scalpel blade
options.D: Mogen clamp

explanation: That's the Plastibell! It stays snug on the tissue, cutting off blood supply to the extra skin so it drops off cleanly after a few days as it heals.

question: During a Gomco clamp procedure, what is the main job of the metal bell component?

options.A: To protect the underlying glans penis from injury during excision
options.B: To deliver continuous local anesthesia throughout the operation
options.C: To hold the urinary catheter securely inside the bladder
options.D: To measure the exact length of the penile shaft

explanation: The metal bell acts like a shield, fitting right over the sensitive glans to keep it safe from the scalpel and the tight clamp.

question: Why are infants gently placed in a restraining board or wrap during a circumcision?

options.A: To keep their body temperature elevated during the operation
options.B: To make it easier for the surgeon to place a urinary catheter
options.C: To prevent sudden movements that could lead to accidental injury
options.D: To stop them from crying out loudly during the procedure

explanation: Babies can't sit still on command! Soft restraints keep them safe and steady so the doctor can work safely with sharp instruments.

question: While local anesthesia is given during the procedure, what is a key thing for the nurse to watch out for?

options.A: Applying pressure dressings before the surgeon cuts the foreskin
options.B: Checking that the local anesthetic solution is heated to body temperature
options.C: Watching for signs of systemic toxicity like changes in breathing or alertness
options.D: Recording the exact time the patient falls into a deep sleep

explanation: You're doing great. If a local anesthetic gets absorbed too quickly into the bloodstream, it can cause reactions. Monitoring the baby's breathing and alertness keeps them safe.

question: Why is petroleum jelly (Vaseline) gauze usually placed on the wound after a circumcision?

options.A: To dissolve any remaining surgical stitches instantly
options.B: To speed up the natural growth of pubic hair follicles
options.C: To prevent the raw surgical site from sticking to the diaper
options.D: To permanently numb the glans penis against clothing

explanation: Vaseline acts as a gentle, non-stick shield. It keeps the tender healing skin from sticking painfully to the baby's diaper.

question: What is the best approach for managing pain in an infant who has just been circumcised?

options.A: Applying ice packs directly to the bare surgical wound for hours
options.B: Administering strong opioid medications every two hours around the clock
options.C: Keeping the infant awake so they do not feel the post-surgical pain
options.D: Using sweet oral sucrose solution alongside prescribed mild pain relievers

explanation: Sweet sucrose drops combined with safe, mild pain meds (like paracetamol) provide great comfort and pain relief for babies.

question: What is the most common immediate complication to watch for after a male circumcision?

options.A: Hemorrhage
options.B: Total urinary retention
options.C: Erectile dysfunction
options.D: Meatal stenosis

explanation: Because the male genital area has a rich blood supply, bleeding (hemorrhage) is the most frequent acute thing to monitor for right after the procedure.

question: Six hours after a circumcision, you notice steady, active bleeding from the wound edge. What is your FIRST nursing action?

options.A: Soak the entire genital area in warm soapy bath water
options.B: Apply direct, firm pressure to the bleeding site with sterile gauze
options.C: Administer a stat dose of intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.D: Wait patiently to see if the bleeding stops on its own within an hour

explanation: Always start with direct pressure using sterile gauze to control bleeding while you call for the doctor to assist.

question: A mother calls worried about a yellowish crust forming over her baby's healing circumcision. What is this?

options.A: Normal granulation tissue part of the healing process
options.B: Leftover residue from petroleum jelly ointment
options.C: A sign of a severe bacterial wound infection
options.D: Dried urine crystals from frequent wet diapers

explanation: No need to panic! That yellowish film is a normal part of how skin heals down there—reassure the mother it's not pus or an infection.

question: Which sign should you teach a mother to report immediately after taking her baby home from a circumcision?

options.A: The baby is unable to pass urine for many hours after the procedure
options.B: The baby cries briefly when the diaper is changed
options.C: A thin yellowish film is visible on the surface of the glans penis
options.D: The Plastibell ring is still attached on the third day at home

explanation: If a baby can't pee, it could mean swelling is blocking the urethra. That's an urgent sign that needs immediate medical review!

question: Why do nurses give medications through an IV line instead of having the patient swallow a pill?

options.A: It lasts much longer in the bloodstream than oral pills.
options.B: It prevents all known systemic side effects from occurring.
options.C: It is completely painless for every patient receiving treatment.
options.D: It provides a much faster onset of drug action in the body.

explanation: Spot on! Because IV fluids go straight into the bloodstream, the body skips the digestive tract entirely and goes to work right away. You've got this!

question: A patient arrives at the clinic with severe vomiting and dehydration. Why is an IV line started instead of just giving them oral rehydration drinks?

options.A: The patient's digestive tract cannot absorb any liquids safely.
options.B: Oral fluids take too long to reach the stomach lining.
options.C: IV fluids rapidly restore circulating blood volume and correct electrolytes.
options.D: Intravenous fluids taste much better than oral rehydration salts.

explanation: Great thinking! When someone is vomiting heavily, IV fluids are the quickest way to restore circulating blood volume and get their electrolytes balanced safely.

question: Where is the median cubital vein located, which is a favourite spot for starting an IV?

options.A: Near the inside of the ankle joint
options.B: Along the lateral side of the upper arm
options.C: On the back of the hand
options.D: In the antecubital fossa of the elbow

explanation: Exactly! The median cubital vein sits right across the bend of the elbow (the antecubital fossa), making it super accessible for quick IV lines and blood tests.

question: When you gently tap and feel a patient's arm to find a good vein, what should a healthy peripheral vein feel like?

options.A: A hard, rigid cord that does not bounce back
options.B: A soft, bouncy vessel that refills after being pressed
options.C: A deep vessel that cannot be felt but looks dark blue
options.D: A pulsing vessel that moves strongly under the finger

explanation: Spot on! Healthy veins feel spongy, elastic, and refill promptly with blood after you press them. You'll get great at spotting these on the ward!

question: Which of these commonly used IV fluids is classified as an isotonic fluid?

options.A: 0.45% Sodium Chloride
options.B: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.C: 10% Dextrose in Water
options.D: 3% Sodium Chloride

explanation: Well done! Normal saline has a salt and water balance very close to human blood plasma, so it stays nicely inside the vessels without causing weird fluid shifts.

question: A patient has severe brain swelling, and you need a fluid that will draw excess water out of the swollen cells and back into the bloodstream. What type of IV solution do you need?

options.A: Hypoosmolar solution
options.B: Isotonic solution
options.C: Hypertonic solution
options.D: Hypotonic solution

explanation: You got it! Hypertonic fluids are concentrated, creating an osmotic pressure that pulls fluid out of tissue cells and safely back into the blood vessels.

question: Why do we apply a tourniquet to a patient's arm before trying to insert an IV cannula?

options.A: To sterilize the outer skin surface before cleaning
options.B: To completely stop arterial blood flow to the limb
options.C: To numb the local skin area and reduce sharp pain
options.D: To trap venous blood and make the veins swell up

explanation: Exactly! The tourniquet pauses blood from returning to the heart, causing the veins underneath to plump up so they are much easier to see and feel.

question: Why do nurses prefer to use a clear, transparent dressing over an IV insertion site?

options.A: It completely stops the patient from feeling any accidental movement pain.
options.B: It allows the nurse to inspect the skin for redness without removing the cover.
options.C: It keeps the cannula warm so the IV fluid flows much faster.
options.D: It permanently seals the vein shut so no blood can ever leak out.

explanation: Spot on! Clear dressings keep outside germs away while letting you quickly check the site for early signs of swelling or redness without peeling anything back.

question: At what angle should you hold your needle when inserting a peripheral IV cannula through the skin?

options.A: 15 to 30 degrees
options.B: 45 to 60 degrees
options.C: 90 degrees straight down
options.D: 5 to 10 degrees

explanation: Great job! A shallow 15 to 30-degree angle lets you glide smoothly into the vein without accidentally poking right through the back wall of the vessel.

question: During an IV insertion, what lets you know for sure that your needle has successfully entered the vein?

options.A: The infusion bag begins to drip rapidly without any pressure.
options.B: The surrounding skin turns pale and cool to the touch.
options.C: The patient reports a sudden cooling sensation in the arm.
options.D: A flash of blood appears inside the flashback chamber of the device.

explanation: That's right! Seeing that little 'flash' of dark red blood in the chamber is the classic sign that you're in the vein. Beautiful work!

question: When programming an electronic IV infusion pump on the ward, what unit of measurement do you normally use?

options.A: Milliliters per hour (mL/hr)
options.B: Liters per 24 hours (L/day)
options.C: Drops per minute (gtt/min)
options.D: Drops per second (gtt/sec)

explanation: Spot on! Pumps are designed to deliver a precise volume of fluid every hour, so we program them in mL/hr.

question: You need to run 1000 mL of normal saline over 8 hours using a manual gravity tubing set with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the approximate flow rate in drops per minute?

options.A: 31 gtt/min
options.B: 125 gtt/min
options.C: 21 gtt/min
options.D: 42 gtt/min

explanation: You're doing great with math! Multiply 1000 mL by 15 to get 15,000 drops, then divide by 480 total minutes (8 hours x 60 mins). That gives you roughly 31 drops per minute!

question: As a student nurse, how often should you check and inspect an active peripheral IV site on your patient?

options.A: Once every 48 hours during dressing changes
options.B: Only when the patient complains of severe pain
options.C: Only when the infusion bag runs completely empty
options.D: At least once every nursing shift

explanation: Exactly! Regular checks each shift help you catch tiny problems like early swelling or soreness before they turn into bigger issues.

question: Why do nurses flush an intermittent IV line with normal saline right after giving a medication?

options.A: To clear remaining drug residue and prevent line clotting
options.B: To dilute any air bubbles that entered during the injection
options.C: To numb the vein so the patient feels less soreness
options.D: To cool down the internal walls of the plastic tubing

explanation: Well done! Flushing pushes any leftover medication completely through the catheter, keeping the line clear and preventing clots.

question: Which of these signs is the classic giveaway that an IV has 'infiltrated' (leaked into the tissue)?

options.A: A warm, red, hard streak running all the way up the arm
options.B: Severe chest pain accompanied by audible lung crackles
options.C: Bright red bleeding gushing out around the plastic catheter
options.D: Swelling, coolness, and pallor around the insertion site

explanation: Spot on! When IV fluid leaks into the tissue instead of the vein, it makes the skin look pale, feel cool, and swell up. Time to restart the line!

question: A patient receiving a strong chemotherapy drug through a peripheral IV suddenly complains of a burning pain, and the area starts swelling up. What is your very first action?

options.A: Stop the infusion immediately and disconnect the tubing.
options.B: Flush the IV line rapidly with normal saline to clear the drug.
options.C: Massage the arm firmly to help the drug spread out faster.
options.D: Apply a cold ice pack directly over the swollen area.

explanation: Safety first! Stopping the infusion right away prevents any more harsh fluid from leaking into the tissue and causing damage.

question: Why must you always inspect the tip of an IV catheter immediately after taking it out of a patient's arm?

options.A: To see if the patient's blood type has changed during therapy
options.B: To test the sterility of the plastic surface before disposal
options.C: To check if the plastic tip broke off inside the vein
options.D: To measure how much blood remains inside the hollow needle

explanation: Great nursing habit! Always check the removed cannula to make sure the entire plastic tip came out cleanly and nothing was left behind.

question: What is the proper technique for pulling a peripheral IV cannula out of a patient's skin?

options.A: Pull it out smoothly and parallel to the skin surface.
options.B: Twist the catheter in a full circle before lifting it out.
options.C: Tug it quickly and firmly to make the removal as fast as possible.
options.D: Pull it straight up toward the ceiling at a sharp 90-degree angle.

explanation: You've got it! Pulling it out smoothly and low to the skin prevents unnecessary scratching or trauma to the fragile vein wall.

question: What is the main focus of cancer epidemiology?

options.A: Testing new chemotherapy drugs in the laboratory
options.B: Studying cancer patterns and causes in populations
options.C: Performing surgical removal of malignant tumors
options.D: Providing daily bedside care to cancer patients

explanation: Cancer epidemiology looks at whole groups of people to see how and why cancer occurs in different populations. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why do public health planners rely on epidemiological data?

options.A: To decide where to direct health resources and programs
options.B: To diagnose individual patients in emergency rooms
options.C: To write personal care plans for recovering clients
options.D: To determine the exact cost of hospital equipment

explanation: Population data helps health authorities see where disease rates are highest so they can build facilities and plan interventions accordingly. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which cancer is the most common among Nigerian women?

options.A: Liver cancer
options.B: Breast cancer
options.C: Cervical cancer
options.D: Ovarian cancer

explanation: Breast cancer is recorded as the leading malignancy among women in Nigeria and globally. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is a major viral infection linked closely to cervical cancer in Nigeria?

options.A: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
options.B: Hepatitis B virus
options.C: Epstein-Barr virus
options.D: Human Papillomavirus

explanation: Persistent infection with high-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus is the primary driver behind most cervical cancer cases. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What does incidence measure in a population?

options.A: The number of new cases diagnosed
options.B: The total number of existing cases
options.C: The percentage of people who die
options.D: The cost of treating the disease

explanation: Incidence specifically counts the new diagnoses appearing over a set timeframe, showing the rate at which a disease develops. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: A public health nurse wants to know the total burden of chronic leukemia in a community, including people diagnosed years ago. Which measure should she look at?

options.A: Risk ratio
options.B: Prevalence
options.C: Incidence
options.D: Mortality rate

explanation: Prevalence measures all existing cases at a given time, capturing both new diagnoses and survivors living with the condition. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following is a non-modifiable risk factor for cancer?

options.A: Smoking
options.B: Alcohol use
options.C: Diet
options.D: Age

explanation: Age is an inherent biological factor that cannot be altered, making it non-modifiable. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why are infectious agents like Hepatitis B classified as cancer risk factors?

options.A: They immediately destroy all red blood cells in the body
options.B: They lower body temperature and stop normal digestion
options.C: They block the absorption of vital nutrients in the gut
options.D: They cause chronic inflammation and cellular damage over time

explanation: Certain viruses and bacteria lead to long-term tissue damage and inflammation, which increases the chance of cellular mutations. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the origin of most cancer-causing mutations?

options.A: Passed down exclusively through maternal bloodlines
options.B: Inherited directly from parents in every single diagnosed case
options.C: Acquired over a lifetime from environmental and lifestyle factors
options.D: Caused entirely by sudden bacterial infections in childhood

explanation: Most cancers arise from acquired mutations that build up over time due to exposure to external agents like tobacco, radiation, and unhealthy diets. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why do people with the same genetic background sometimes have different cancer risks?

options.A: Genetics is the only factor that ever influences disease
options.B: Inherited genes change completely every five years
options.C: Their environmental exposures and lifestyle choices vary
options.D: Lifestyle habits have no real impact on cellular health

explanation: Environmental and lifestyle factors interact with genes, meaning different habits will alter overall risk even among family members. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of cancer screening programs?

options.A: To replace traditional biopsy procedures entirely
options.B: To detect cancer or precancerous changes early
options.C: To cure late-stage metastatic disease completely
options.D: To measure the exact cost of hospital stays

explanation: Screening aims to identify disease before symptoms appear so treatment can start when it is most effective. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: A community health nurse is planning a cervical cancer screening outreach. Which test is she most likely to utilize?

options.A: Liver biopsy
options.B: Chest X-ray
options.C: Pap smear
options.D: Prostate-specific antigen test

explanation: A Pap smear is a standard, widely used screening tool for detecting cervical cell abnormalities and precancerous lesions. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: How do nurses directly help with cancer epidemiology in clinical and community settings?

options.A: Funding public health research grants through private banks
options.B: Designing blueprints for modern oncology radiation bunkers
options.C: Manufacturing new chemotherapy drugs in hospital pharmacies
options.D: Accurate data collection and maintaining cancer registries

explanation: Nurses play a huge role by gathering precise patient data and keeping records updated, which helps researchers track cancer trends. You're making great progress! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why are community health nurses in a great position to promote cancer prevention?

options.A: They are the only healthcare professionals permitted to diagnose tumors
options.B: They hold exclusive authority over national public health budgets
options.C: They interact directly with individuals and families on a regular basis
options.D: They spend all their time working inside high-tech molecular laboratories

explanation: Because nurses interact regularly with everyday people and families, they are perfectly placed to teach about risk factors and encourage healthy habits. Well done! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary objective of a debulking surgical procedure in cancer management?

options.A: To replace damaged lymph nodes entirely
options.B: To reduce tumor mass to ease symptoms
options.C: To completely cure the client of the disease
options.D: To deliver systemic localized radiation

explanation: Debulking surgery does not remove the entire tumor, but reducing its size helps alleviate pressure on surrounding organs and makes subsequent treatments more effective. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why does chemotherapy frequently cause side effects in healthy, rapidly dividing tissues like hair follicles and the gastrointestinal tract?

options.A: Systemic drugs accumulate preferentially in the superficial layers of the skin.
options.B: Chemotherapy agents selectively target only benign metabolic pathways.
options.C: Chemotherapy stimulates the immune system to attack normal mucosal cells.
options.D: Normal tissues share the rapid cellular division characteristic of cancer cells.

explanation: Cytotoxic drugs are designed to target cells undergoing frequent division, which inadvertently damages healthy rapidly proliferating cells in the bone marrow, gut, and hair follicles. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h1)

question: What is a primary reason for enforcing early ambulation in a client recovering from major oncological surgery?

options.A: To eliminate the need for postoperative analgesic medications
options.B: To prevent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
options.C: To stimulate immediate resumption of normal bowel motility
options.D: To accelerate the complete closure of surgical incision sites

explanation: Early ambulation promotes venous return in the lower extremities, significantly reducing the risk of blood stasis and subsequent clot formation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h2)

question: A client returns to the surgical ward following a radical neck dissection for laryngeal cancer. Which immediate nursing action is most critical?

options.A: Administering a prescribed high-protein oral diet
options.B: Encouraging the client to perform vigorous neck range of motion
options.C: Removing the primary surgical drains to check for bleeding
options.D: Assessing airway patency and monitoring for neck swelling

explanation: Surgeries around the neck area carry a high risk of airway compromise due to localized edema, hematoma formation, or tracheal displacement, making airway surveillance the top priority. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h2)

question: What term describes a chemotherapy medication capable of causing severe tissue destruction and necrosis if it leaks into subcutaneous tissue?

options.A: A vesicant
options.B: A radiolabel
options.C: A pyrogen
options.D: Anantagonist

explanation: Vesicants are highly irritating cytotoxic agents that cause blistering and deep tissue damage upon accidental extravasation into peripheral tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is the appropriate initial nursing action if a client receiving a peripheral intravenous infusion of a vesicant chemotherapy agent reports a burning sensation at the needle site?

options.A: Immediately stop the infusion and disconnect the intravenous tubing
options.B: Administer a topical analgesic cream over the injection site
options.C: Flush the peripheral line rapidly with normal saline to clear the drug
options.D: Slow the infusion rate down and apply a warm compress

explanation: Stopping the infusion immediately limits the amount of drug entering the interstitial tissue, preventing further localized damage before institutional extravasation protocols are initiated. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h3)

question: Which instruction should a nurse give to a client undergoing external beam radiation therapy regarding skin markings?

options.A: Apply petroleum jelly directly over the markings every morning
options.B: Scrub the markings daily with alcohol to prevent skin infection
options.C: Cover the markings completely with adhesive waterproof bandages
options.D: Avoid washing off or altering the temporary ink markings

explanation: Radiation ink tattoos or markings are essential for ensuring the precise alignment of the radiation beam during every treatment session and must be preserved. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h4)

question: What is a recommended practice for skin hygiene within a radiation treatment field?

options.A: Applying heating pads to soothe localized radiation erythema
options.B: Wearing tight synthetic garments to protect the skin from air
options.C: Using scented commercial soaps and vigorous washcloth friction
options.D: Washing gently with lukewarm water and patting the skin dry

explanation: Gentle cleansing with mild water and patting dry prevents mechanical irritation to fragile, radiation-damaged epidermal layers. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h4)

question: Which nursing intervention is most appropriate for a client experiencing chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia?

options.A: Instructing the client to shave facial hair using an electric razor
options.B: Administering intramuscular injections for routine pain relief
options.C: Encouraging the use of hard-bristled toothbrushes for plaque removal
options.D: Applying firm pressure dressings over all venipuncture sites for an hour

explanation: Electric razors minimize the risk of accidental skin nicks and bleeding in clients with low platelet counts, whereas straight razors and intramuscular injections should be avoided. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is the single most reliable early indicator of infection in a client experiencing severe neutropenia?

options.A: An elevated core body temperature or fever
options.B: Severe localized pain in the lower abdomen
options.C: A sudden drop in systemic blood pressure
options.D: Purulent drainage visible at a surgical site

explanation: Because neutropenic clients lack sufficient neutrophils to mount a standard inflammatory response, even a mild fever can be the only sign of a potentially fatal systemic infection. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h5)

question: What clinical manifestation is most characteristic of Superior Vena Cava Syndrome?

options.A: Facial edema, periorbital swelling, and jugular vein distention
options.B: Bilateral paralysis of the lower extremities
options.C: Severe lower extremity pitting edema and calf pain
options.D: Acute left upper quadrant abdominal tenderness

explanation: Obstruction of blood flow through the superior vena cava causes venous congestion in the upper body, resulting in characteristic facial and neck swelling. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which metabolic abnormalities are classically associated with Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Hypokalemia, hypouricemia, and hypercalcemia
options.B: Hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, and hyperphosphatemia
options.C: Hyperkalemia, hypouricemia, and hypophosphatemia
options.D: Hyponatremia, hypophosphatemia, and hypercalcemia

explanation: The massive lysis of cancer cells releases large amounts of potassium, nucleic acids that metabolize into uric acid, and phosphorus directly into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is cancer cachexia primarily characterized by?

options.A: Rapid accumulation of subcutaneous adipose tissue
options.B: Excessive appetite and elevated serum albumin levels
options.C: Progressive involuntary weight loss and muscle wasting
options.D: Severe fluid retention and generalized anasarca

explanation: Cancer cachexia is a wasting syndrome driven by metabolic alterations and systemic inflammation that causes severe loss of skeletal muscle and fat mass that cannot be reversed by conventional nutrition alone. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h7)

question: Which dietary modification is most effective for a client experiencing severe cancer-related anorexia and early satiety?

options.A: Serving three large, highly spiced meals daily at standard times
options.B: Offering low-calorie liquid clear broths to stimulate digestion
options.C: Restricting fluid intake entirely during all waking hours
options.D: Encouraging small, frequent meals high in calories and protein

explanation: Small, nutrient-dense portions prevent the client from feeling overwhelmed by large quantities of food while maximizing caloric and protein intake. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h7)

question: At what point in the disease trajectory should palliative care ideally be introduced for a client with advanced cancer?

options.A: Only when all curative medical treatments have failed
options.B: Simultaneously alongside active disease-directed treatments
options.C: After the client is discharged to hospice care at home
options.D: Strictly during the final forty-eight hours of life

explanation: Modern palliative care is designed to be integrated early in the disease course alongside curative therapies to manage symptoms and improve overall quality of life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of nursing interventions when providing psychosocial support to a newly diagnosed cancer client?

options.A: Discouraging discussion about terminal outcomes or death
options.B: Encouraging active listening and validating emotional responses
options.C: Redirecting conversation away from personal fears toward diet
options.D: Offering immediate guarantees of complete remission

explanation: Creating a safe space for clients to express their fears through active listening helps process complex emotions and reduces feelings of isolation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: To eliminate the need for routine pharmacological pain management
options.B: To restore or maintain functional independence and quality of life
options.C: To accelerate the physiological elimination of chemotherapy agents
options.D: To provide curative medical therapy for primary malignancies

explanation: Cancer rehabilitation focuses on maximizing physical, social, and psychological functioning rather than directly treating the underlying tumor. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h1)

question: Which professional is primarily responsible for helping patients relearn skills needed for daily living activities?

options.A: Occupational therapist
options.B: Oncology social worker
options.C: Diagnostic radiographer
options.D: Clinical research coordinator

explanation: Occupational therapists focus on adapting environments and retraining patients in activities of daily living like dressing, bathing, and eating. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team essential in cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: Hospital accreditation standards require a minimum of six distinct specialties per patient
options.B: Physicians lack the legal authority to prescribe physical exercise regimens
options.C: Cancer and its treatments affect multiple physical and psychosocial body systems simultaneously
options.D: Multidisciplinary models completely eliminate the risk of chronic treatment side effects

explanation: The complex multisystem impact of malignancy requires diverse professional expertise to provide holistic, effective care. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of utilizing standardized performance scales like ECOG in oncology?

options.A: To measure the exact histological grade of a tumor
options.B: To determine the financial cost of prolonged hospitalization
options.C: To quantify a patient's functional ability and independence
options.D: To calculate the precise metabolic clearance of chemotherapy

explanation: Performance scales provide objective measurements of how cancer affects daily functioning and systemic well-being. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: A comprehensive patient assessment in cancer rehabilitation MUST include evaluation of which of the following areas? (Select the best overall answer)

options.A: Physical, psychological, and environmental factors
options.B: Prior occupational history without current functional status
options.C: Exclusively laboratory and hematological parameters
options.D: Only the direct cost of surgical interventions

explanation: Holistic assessment requires evaluating bodily systems, mental health, and home or social contexts to design an effective care plan. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: How does cancer-related fatigue primarily differ from ordinary fatigue?

options.A: It is caused strictly by underlying electrolyte imbalances
options.B: It responds immediately to high-carbohydrate dietary intake
options.C: It exclusively occurs during the late evening hours
options.D: It is not relieved by restorative sleep or rest

explanation: Cancer-related fatigue is persistent, subjective, and disproportionate to recent activity levels, failing to improve with standard rest. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is a recommended non-pharmacological intervention to help manage cancer-related fatigue?

options.A: Complete strict bedrest until treatment ends
options.B: Elimination of all daytime fluid intake
options.C: High-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy
options.D: Regular, moderate-intensity physical exercise

explanation: Structured aerobic activity has been clinically proven to reduce the severity of cancer-related fatigue and improve overall energy levels. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: Which clinical parameter must be carefully reviewed prior to initiating high-impact physical therapy in patients with bone metastases?

options.A: Baseline renal glomerular filtration rate
options.B: Fasting serum blood glucose concentrations
options.C: Structural bone integrity and fracture risk
options.D: Patient blood type and Rh factor status

explanation: Bone metastases weaken skeletal structures, requiring modified, low-impact exercise prescriptions to prevent pathological fractures. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is a primary benefit of resistance training in cancer rehabilitation programs?

options.A: Preventing the cellular mutation of benign tumors
options.B: Reversing cancer-induced skeletal muscle wasting and weakness
options.C: Accelerating the renal excretion of radiation contrast
options.D: Completely curing localized peripheral nerve damage

explanation: Resistance exercises stimulate muscle protein synthesis, combating cachexia and generalized physical deconditioning. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: What term describes the complex wasting syndrome associated with advanced cancer characterized by severe muscle and weight loss?

options.A: Metabolic alkalosis
options.B: Hyperosmolar dehydration
options.C: Cancer cachexia
options.D: Sarcopenic obesity

explanation: Cachexia is a multifactorial wasting syndrome driven by systemic inflammation and altered metabolism that does not respond fully to standard nutritional repletion. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why is early nutritional intervention critical during active oncological treatment?

options.A: It guarantees complete tumor regression without adjuvant medical therapy
options.B: It prevents the development of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
options.C: It preserves lean body mass and improves tolerance to chemotherapy or radiation
options.D: It eliminates the need for intravenous access lines during surgery

explanation: Maintaining optimal nutritional status helps patients withstand high-dose therapies and reduces treatment interruptions caused by severe debility. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is a primary component of a comprehensive survivorship care plan?

options.A: A structured schedule for recurrence monitoring and late-effect surveillance
options.B: An official prescription waiver for outpatient analgesic drugs
options.C: A legal document transferring medical decision-making to family members
options.D: A binding employment contract for workplace readjustment

explanation: Survivorship care plans outline follow-up imaging, clinical evaluations, and guidance on managing potential long-term treatment side effects. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: Which psychological concern is most commonly experienced by individuals transitioning into long-term cancer survivorship?

options.A: Severe acute delirium mimicking acute intoxication
options.B: Persistent anxiety regarding cancer recurrence
options.C: Complete denial of ever having received a diagnosis
options.D: Total indifference toward routine health monitoring

explanation: The fear of cancer returning is a widespread and enduring challenge for survivors long after active treatment concludes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary characteristic that distinguishes malignant neoplasms from benign neoplasms?

options.A: The ability to invade surrounding tissues and metastasize
options.B: The tendency to spontaneously resolve without medical treatment
options.C: Slow and localized growth patterns within a single organ
options.D: A complete absence of blood vessel supply within the mass

explanation: Malignant neoplasms are defined by their capacity to break through basement membranes, invade adjacent structures, and spread to distant sites, whereas benign tumors remain localized. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is early prevention emphasized so strongly in resource-limited healthcare settings like Nigeria?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs are always less effective than lifestyle modifications
options.B: Advanced-stage presentation is very common and harder to treat successfully
options.C: Preventive measures completely eliminate the genetic risk of all cancers
options.D: Surgical interventions are entirely unavailable for treating localized tumors

explanation: When patients present late in the disease course, treatment options become more complex, expensive, and less likely to result in a cure, making prevention paramount. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which nursing intervention represents a primary prevention strategy against cervical cancer?

options.A: Performing a routine Papanicolaou (Pap) smear screening
options.B: Administering the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine
options.C: Providing postoperative care following a radical hysterectomy
options.D: Instructing a patient on managing chemotherapy-induced nausea

explanation: Vaccines prevent the initial viral infection that leads to cellular changes, classifying immunization as primary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: A community health nurse is designing a seminar to reduce cancer risk factors. Which topic should be included as a primary prevention measure?

options.A: Techniques for performing monthly self-examinations of the breast
options.B: Strategies for quitting cigarette smoking and avoiding tobacco
options.C: Managing chronic fatigue during systemic cancer chemotherapy
options.D: Interpreting the results of a routine prostate-specific antigen test

explanation: Avoiding known carcinogens like tobacco prevents cellular damage and mutation from occurring in the first place, fulfilling primary prevention goals. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: What is the primary objective of secondary prevention activities in oncology?

options.A: Rehabilitation and palliation of end-stage metastatic illness
options.B: Complete prevention of initial cellular mutation events
options.C: Early detection and prompt treatment of asymptomatic disease
options.D: Elimination of environmental radiation and chemical hazards

explanation: Secondary prevention aims to catch neoplastic changes early when intervention can halt disease progression before symptoms appear. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: A 45-year-old female patient visits a primary health clinic asking how to check for breast cancer before she feels any lumps. Which nursing response describes a secondary prevention action?

options.A: Providing comfort measures and emotional support for a patient undergoing radiation therapy
options.B: Discussing the recommended schedule for screening mammograms and clinical breast exams
options.C: Explaining how avoiding alcohol consumption decreases long-term breast cancer risk
options.D: Administering prophylactic antibiotics to prevent opportunistic infections during treatment

explanation: Mammograms and clinical breast examinations are standard screening tools used to detect tumors early, defining secondary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: Which activity is classified as a tertiary prevention intervention in cancer care?

options.A: Administering routine HPV vaccinations to teenage school children
options.B: Managing lymphedema and physical therapy following a mastectomy
options.C: Conducting community outreach lectures on the dangers of smoking
options.D: Performing a routine screening colonoscopy on an asymptomatic adult

explanation: Tertiary prevention deals with rehabilitation and minimizing disability after the disease and its primary treatments have occurred. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why is long-term follow-up care considered a crucial aspect of tertiary prevention for cancer survivors?

options.A: It guarantees that the patient will never experience lifestyle alterations again
options.B: It allows early identification of disease recurrence or secondary malignancies
options.C: It eliminates all financial and social burdens associated with the illness
options.D: It replaces the need for primary prevention education within the community

explanation: Survivors remain at risk for relapse or new primary cancers, making ongoing surveillance a key tertiary prevention strategy to catch issues early. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse when a family history suggests a strong hereditary cancer syndrome?

options.A: Performing genetic laboratory sequencing directly at the bedside
options.B: Ordering prophylactic surgical removal of organs without consultation
options.C: Telling the family that inherited gene mutations cannot be tested
options.D: Recognizing patterns and facilitating a referral for genetic counseling

explanation: Nurses identify at-risk families during health history assessments and connect them with specialized genetic counselors for comprehensive risk evaluation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: Which action demonstrates effective patient education by a nurse caring for an individual undergoing cancer treatment?

options.A: Limiting educational conversations to written pamphlets without verbal discussion
options.B: Providing a highly technical research journal article for the patient to read independently
options.C: Assessing the patient's literacy level and tailoring explanations about side effect management
options.D: Assuming the patient understands all discharge instructions if they nod politely

explanation: Effective education requires evaluating the learner's needs and communication barriers to ensure comprehension of self-care and warning signs. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why must nurses engage in community advocacy and public health policy regarding cancer prevention?

options.A: Advocacy is solely the responsibility of hospital administrators and physicians
options.B: Government agencies prohibit individual nurses from educating patients directly
options.C: Bedside nursing care has been proven to completely replace the need for public health laws
options.D: Systemic factors like environmental hazards and policy gaps significantly impact population health

explanation: Policy and environmental conditions dictate exposure risks and healthcare access, making broader advocacy essential for sustainable disease prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h6)

question: A public health nurse in a rural Nigerian community notices that many women refuse breast screening due to cultural stigma and fear. Which advocacy action is most appropriate?

options.A: Ignoring the cultural beliefs since they do not affect clinical screening outcomes
options.B: Focusing entirely on acute inpatient chemotherapy administration in urban hospitals
options.C: Passing strict municipal laws that fine individuals who fail to attend annual health clinics
options.D: Partnering with local community leaders and religious heads to conduct culturally sensitive awareness campaigns

explanation: Working with respected community figures helps address stigma and fatalism, improving health literacy and screening acceptance in local populations. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h6)

question: What is the primary underlying cause of oncologic emergencies?

options.A: Acute or chronic complications directly or indirectly related to malignancy or therapy
options.B: Acquired immunodeficiency unrelated to the primary tumor or treatment
options.C: Long-term side effects occurring years after successful cancer remission
options.D: Primary psychiatric disorders triggered by a terminal cancer diagnosis

explanation: These emergencies stem directly from tumor growth, metabolic changes caused by cancer cells, or toxicities from aggressive treatment regimens. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why do many patients in resource-limited settings frequently present with advanced oncologic emergencies?

options.A: Strict adherence to prophylactic metabolic suppression medications
options.B: Delays in initial presentation resulting in bulky, untreated disease masses
options.C: Over-prescription of outpatient chemotherapy by community pharmacists
options.D: Excessive availability of routine screening programs in rural areas

explanation: Late presentation with large tumor volumes significantly increases the likelihood of structural compression and metabolic crises. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h1)

question: Which electrolyte abnormality is a defining hallmark of Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Hypokalemia
options.B: Hyperkalemia
options.C: Hypomagnesemia
options.D: Hyponatremia

explanation: The massive destruction of cancer cells releases large amounts of intracellular potassium directly into the systemic circulation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary mechanism behind Hypercalcemia of Malignancy?

options.A: Excessive dietary calcium intake by patients undergoing palliative cancer care
options.B: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein leading to increased bone resorption
options.C: Kidney failure causing immediate retention of dietary calcium ions
options.D: Complete failure of the parathyroid glands due to metastatic infiltration

explanation: Certain tumors secrete PTHrP or cause direct osteolytic destruction, driving excessive calcium out of the bones and into the blood. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: What is typically the earliest clinical symptom of Malignant Spinal Cord Compression?

options.A: Inability to feel temperature
options.B: Progressive back pain
options.C: Sudden complete paralysis
options.D: Loss of bowel control

explanation: Back pain often precedes neurological deficits by weeks and should be investigated urgently in any patient with a cancer history. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h3)

question: Which physical finding is most characteristic of Superior Vena Cava Syndrome?

options.A: Tracheal deviation to the left side
options.B: Marked lower extremity pitting edema
